slot.brief: Show a Fischer projection of a chiral molecule in the figure; assign R/S after a stated 90° rotation of the projection and identify the enantiomer/diastereomer among options.

stem: The Fischer projection is rotated clockwise by $90^\circ$ in its plane and then read as a Fischer projection. What configuration and relationship to the original does it represent?

verdicts.working: The depicted molecule is (2S,3S). Rotating a Fischer projection by 90° and reading it again as a Fischer projection inverts both stereocenters, giving (2R,3R), the enantiomer.
issues: The figure is a wedge-dash structure, not a Fischer projection; it does provide enough stereochemical information to determine the molecule's configuration.

working:
Original Fischer: at C2, priorities are OH $>$ CHO $>$ C3 $>$ H; at C3, OH $>$ C2 $>$ CH3 $>$ H.
In each centre, H is horizontal, so reverse the observed order: both centres are $S$.
A $90^\circ$ rotation swaps the horizontal and vertical substituents at each centre.
Thus both configurations invert: $(2S,3S) \to (2R,3R)$.
Both stereocentres invert, so the result is the enantiomer.

Independent check: The depicted molecule is (2S,3S). Rotating a Fischer projection by 90° and reading it again as a Fischer projection inverts both stereocenters, giving (2R,3R), the enantiomer.
solution:
In the original Fischer projection, both centres are $(S)$; a $90^\circ$ rotation swaps horizontal and vertical substituents, inverting each centre.
$$
(2S,3S)\longrightarrow(2R,3R)
$$
Both stereocentres invert, so the rotated structure is the enantiomer.

figure.description: Draw a Fischer projection as a vertical carbon chain: CHO at the top, then stereocentre C2, then stereocentre C3, then CH3 at the bottom. At each stereocentre, draw OH on the left and H on the right. Label the two stereocentres C2 and C3. Use horizontal bonds for the left and right substituents and vertical bonds for the chain.
